title: Interfaces vs Type Aliases
description: When to reach for `interface` versus `type` when modeling shapes.

blocks.content: Both `interface` and `type` describe the shape of an object, and are largely interchangeable for that use case. Interfaces support declaration merging (re-opening the same interface adds to it) and are generally preferred for public object/class APIs. Type aliases can also describe unions, tuples, and primitives, which interfaces cannot.
keyPoints: Only `interface` supports declaration merging.
Only `type` can alias unions, intersections, tuples, and primitives directly.
A class can `implements` an interface or a type alias that describes an object shape.

blocks.question: When would you choose `type` over `interface`?
blocks.answer: When you need to model a union, a tuple, a mapped/conditional type, or any non-object shape — interfaces can only describe object-like shapes.
blocks.explanation: For plain object contracts, either works; many teams pick one as a house style and reserve the other for cases only it can express.

blocks.question: You're writing a library and want consumers to be able to add new properties to one of your exported interfaces (e.g. augmenting a global `Window` or a plugin config type). Would you export it as an `interface` or a `type`, and why?
blocks.answer: As an `interface` — declaration merging means a consumer can write another `interface Window { myPlugin: MyPlugin }` in their own code and TypeScript merges it into the original, adding the property. A `type` alias can't be reopened like this; redeclaring it is a compile error.
blocks.explanation: This is exactly how libraries like Express (`Request` augmentation) and Angular itself extend ambient global types — it's one of the few places the interface-vs-type choice isn't just style, it's a hard capability difference.

blocks.content: A union type (`A | B`) accepts a value that is either A or B, and only members common to both are accessible without narrowing. An intersection type (`A & B`) requires a value that satisfies both A and B simultaneously — all members of both are accessible.
keyPoints: Narrow a union with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, or a discriminant property before accessing type-specific members.
Intersecting two object types merges their properties; intersecting incompatible primitive types (e.g. `string & number`) produces `never`.
Discriminated unions (a shared literal `type` field) are the idiomatic way to model variant data in TypeScript.

blocks.question: What is the type of `merged` here?
blocks.explanation: Intersecting A and B combines their members; since `id` is compatible (`string` in both), the result requires both `id` and `label`.

blocks.question: Given `type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | { kind: 'square'; side: number }`, why does `shape.radius` error even after checking `if ('radius' in shape)`?
blocks.answer: It doesn't error — the `in` operator is actually a valid TypeScript narrowing technique for unions that *don't* share a common discriminant property, and `if ('radius' in shape)` correctly narrows `shape` to the circle branch, making `.radius` safe to access.
blocks.explanation: This is a common point of confusion: people assume only `switch (shape.kind)` narrows unions, but `in`, `typeof`, `instanceof`, and custom type-guard functions (`function isCircle(s): s is Circle`) are all valid narrowing mechanisms — the discriminant-field pattern (`kind`) is just the most ergonomic one when you control the shape's design.

title: Generics
description: Writing reusable, type-safe functions and classes parameterized over types.

blocks.content: Generics let a function, interface, or class defer the concrete type until it is used, while still preserving type relationships between inputs and outputs. A generic constraint (`<T extends SomeShape>`) restricts which types are allowed while still letting the compiler infer the specific type used at each call site.
keyPoints: `function first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined` preserves the element type of whatever array is passed in.
`<T extends { id: string }>` constrains T to object types that at least have an `id` string field.
Generic defaults (`<T = string>`) provide a fallback type when the caller doesn't specify one.

blocks.explanation: The function works for any array type T while the return type stays precisely tied to both T and the key type K.

blocks.question: Why use a generic constraint like `<T extends { id: string }>` instead of just typing the parameter as `any`?
blocks.answer: The constraint preserves full type information and IDE autocompletion for the caller's specific type while still guaranteeing the function can safely access `.id`; `any` throws away all type safety entirely.
blocks.explanation: Generics give you both flexibility (works with many types) and safety (the compiler still checks usage), which `any` cannot provide.

blocks.question: What does TypeScript infer for `T` in each call, and does the second call compile?
blocks.answer: `a` infers T as `number` (type `number[]`) and compiles fine. `b` explicitly pins T to `string`, so passing `42` (a number) is a type error — argument of type 'number' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'.
blocks.explanation: Generic type arguments can always be inferred from usage, or supplied explicitly with `<T>` syntax to override inference — but once supplied explicitly, the compiler holds every argument to that pinned type instead of inferring it freely.

title: Utility Types
description: Built-in type transformations like Partial, Pick, Omit, and Record.

blocks.content: TypeScript ships mapped-type helpers that transform an existing type instead of redefining it by hand: `Partial<T>` makes every property optional, `Required<T>` makes every property mandatory, `Pick<T, K>` selects a subset of keys, `Omit<T, K>` removes a subset of keys, and `Record<K, V>` builds an object type with keys K and values V.
keyPoints: `Partial<Topic>` is useful for PATCH-style update payloads where any subset of fields may be supplied.
`Pick<Topic, 'id' | 'title'>` extracts a lightweight summary type derived from a larger interface.
`Record<string, TopicProgress>` models a dictionary keyed by topic id, exactly as used in the Progress Store.

blocks.question: What does the resulting type look like?
blocks.code:
interface Topic { id: string; title: string; difficulty: string; }
type TopicPreview = Omit<Topic, 'difficulty'>;
blocks.explanation: Omit removes the listed keys ('difficulty') from the source type, keeping everything else unchanged.

blocks.question: You have a function `function computeMetrics(subjects: Subject[]): DashboardMetrics { ... }` but no exported type for its return value. How do you get a usable type for `DashboardMetrics` without duplicating the shape by hand?
blocks.answer: `type Metrics = ReturnType<typeof computeMetrics>;` — ReturnType extracts a function's return type, and Parameters<typeof computeMetrics> would similarly extract a tuple type of its parameters.
blocks.explanation: ReturnType and Parameters are two of the most practically useful utility types for keeping derived types in sync with implementation — if computeMetrics's return shape changes, `Metrics` updates automatically instead of silently drifting out of date like a hand-written duplicate would.

title: keyof and typeof
description: Deriving types from the shape of existing types and values.

blocks.content: `keyof T` produces a union of T's property names as string/number literal types. `typeof value` (in a type position) extracts the static type of a runtime value, letting you derive a type from an object literal or a const array instead of writing it twice.
keyPoints: `keyof Topic` yields `'id' | 'title' | 'difficulty' | ...` for every key of Topic.
`typeof STORAGE_KEYS` combined with indexed access can derive the union of storage key string values.
Combining both lets you write generic, type-safe accessor functions like `get<K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K]`.

blocks.explanation: `as const` narrows the object's values to literal types, and `keyof typeof` derives a precise union of those literal string values.

blocks.question: What is the type of `difficulty` here?
blocks.explanation: `Topic['difficulty']` is an indexed access type — it reads the type of a specific property off another type, the same way `topic.difficulty` reads the value off an object at runtime. It's how you derive a narrower type from one field of a larger interface without retyping the union by hand.

title: Discriminated Unions
description: Modeling variant data safely using a shared literal tag field.

blocks.content: A discriminated union gives every variant of a union a shared literal property (a 'tag' or 'discriminant', e.g. `type`), which TypeScript uses to narrow the type inside `if`/`switch` branches without any manual type guard function. This is exactly the pattern used by `ContentBlock` in this application: every block variant shares a `type` field.
keyPoints: Narrowing on the discriminant field works inside `if`, `switch`, and `.filter()` callbacks.
A `default` branch that assigns the remaining value to a `never`-typed variable gives compile-time exhaustiveness checking.
Discriminated unions avoid unsafe type assertions when handling heterogeneous data.

blocks.explanation: If a new ContentBlock variant is added later without a matching case, this function fails to compile because `block` would no longer be assignable to `never` in the default branch.

blocks.question: A teammate adds a fifth PracticeAttempt result — 'skipped' — to the `result: 'correct' | 'incorrect' | 'needs-revision'` union in this app's PracticeAttempt model, but forgets to update the switch statement that renders a badge for each result. Without the exhaustiveness pattern, what happens? With it, what happens?
blocks.answer: Without exhaustiveness checking, the switch statement compiles fine and silently falls through to whatever the default case does (or renders nothing) for 'skipped' — a runtime gap that's easy to miss in review. With a `default: { const check: never = result; ... }` exhaustiveness guard, the same change fails to compile the moment the union grows, forcing the teammate to add a 'skipped' case before the build passes.
blocks.explanation: This is the practical payoff of discriminated unions plus exhaustiveness checking: it turns a class of 'forgot to handle the new case' bugs from a runtime surprise into a compile-time error, at zero runtime cost.

title: unknown vs any
description: Why `unknown` is the type-safe alternative to `any` for values of uncertain shape.

blocks.content: `any` disables type checking entirely for a value — you can call any method or access any property with no compiler errors. `unknown` also accepts any value, but forces you to narrow it (via `typeof`, `instanceof`, or a type guard) before you can do anything with it.
keyPoints: Prefer `unknown` for values from external sources (JSON.parse, imported JSON content) until validated.
`any` silently defeats the type checker for everything that flows through it.
Narrowing `unknown` down to a concrete type is exactly how safely validating imported progress-export JSON should work.

blocks.question: Why does `JSON.parse` return `any` instead of `unknown`, and is that a good default?
blocks.answer: Historically JSON.parse was typed to return `any` for convenience, but it is widely considered a footgun — the safer pattern is to treat the result as `unknown` and validate/narrow it before use.
blocks.explanation: When importing progress data in this application, the parsed JSON should be checked against the expected `StoredApplicationData` shape before being trusted, rather than assumed correct.

blocks.title: Narrowing unknown with a type predicate
blocks.explanation: A function whose return type is `value is StoredApplicationData` (a type predicate) lets you write a runtime check once and get real compile-time narrowing everywhere it's called — this is exactly the pattern DataManagementService.importFromJson uses to safely accept unknown, user-supplied import files.
